questions.learningObjective: apply the doctrine of defences and justification to a concrete legal fact pattern
questions.stem: Consider this: A defendant claiming self-defence argues that force was necessary. The threat had already ended. Which statement best states the governing legal rule?

options.text: Self-defence justifies force that is reasonably necessary to prevent imminent unlawful harm, and the force used must be proportionate to the threat faced for this case.
A person may use deadly force against any perceived threat, however minor on the facts given.
options.misconception: assumes any threat permits deadly force

options.text: Only the defendant's sincere belief matters, even if it was unreasonable in the circumstances.
Force used after the threat has ended is still self-defence in the case at hand.

questions.explanation: The defence has necessity and proportionality limits. A reasonable belief in imminent harm is required, and the response must not exceed what the situation justified; force after the danger has passed becomes retaliation. Here the decisive point is self-defence and proportional force, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask about the imminence of the threat and the amount of force used. Keep the inquiry on self-defence and proportional force.
